analysis.headline: Passed the House 230-192 on December 12, 2019; received in the Senate and placed on the legislative calendar, but never brought to a Senate vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have let the Department of Health and Human Services negotiate maximum prices for the most expensive brand-name drugs that face no generic competition, including insulin. Under current law, HHS is prohibited from negotiating drug prices. The negotiated prices would apply in Medicare and could also apply in private insurance, and the bill added Medicare dental, vision, and hearing coverage, inflation rebates from drugmakers, and a lower out-of-pocket cap for Medicare beneficiaries. It passed the House but never received a vote in the Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, especially those taking expensive brand-name drugs or insulin; low-income Medicare enrollees who would gain subsidy eligibility; seniors who would gain dental, vision, and hearing coverage; people with private insurance if their plans accept the negotiated prices; and communities affected by the opioid epidemic, which would have received dedicated funding.

how_it_helps.text: HHS would negotiate maximum prices for at least 25 single-source brand-name drugs with no generic competition beginning in 2023, rising to at least 50 in 2024, plus all insulin products, selected from the 125 drugs with the greatest national or Medicare spending.

The negotiated maximum price could not exceed 120% of the average price in Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Japan, and the United Kingdom, or, where that data is unavailable, 85% of the U.S. average manufacturer price.
Drugmakers would owe rebates to Medicare for drugs costing $100 or more whose prices rise faster than inflation.
The bill would eliminate beneficiary cost-sharing above a reduced annual out-of-pocket threshold in the Medicare drug benefit and let some enrollees spread cost-sharing payments into installments.
Medicare would be expanded to cover dental and oral health care, hearing aids and hearing treatment, and eyeglasses, contact lenses, and vision services.
The bill expands premium and cost-sharing subsidies for low-income Medicare beneficiaries and lets residents of U.S. territories automatically qualify.

It funds NIH and FDA innovation programs through the end of the decade and creates an Opioid Epidemic Response Fund, and requires direct-to-consumer TV drug ads to display the list price of a 30-day supply.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers. Their products would be subject to government price negotiation, and a manufacturer that refused to negotiate or comply faced an excise tax on sales that starts at 65% of the sale price in the first 90 days of noncompliance and climbs to 95% thereafter, plus civil monetary penalties of up to ten times the difference between the price charged and the negotiated maximum, and fines up to $1 million per violation of agreement terms. Insurers and employers whose plans use the covered drugs would also bear administrative changes, though private plans could opt out of the negotiated prices.

drawbacks.text: Opponents in the House argued the bill should not take effect until the HHS Secretary certifies that its implementation is not projected to result in fewer new drug applications for unmet medical needs and life-saving cures; their motion to recommit with that instruction failed 196-226.

The enforcement mechanism is severe: a manufacturer that does not reach agreement faces an excise tax equal to 65-95% of its sales of the selected drug, which critics could argue functions closer to compelled price-setting than negotiation.

The bill limits judicial review: the selection of drugs for negotiation and the determination of the maximum fair price cannot be challenged in court, leaving manufacturers limited recourse if they contest how prices were set.

The price benefit in private insurance is optional: group health plans and insurers can affirmatively elect not to participate in the program for selected drugs, so consumers outside Medicare are covered only if their plan stays in.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits to Medicare beneficiaries and people on expensive brand-name drugs are direct and large: price caps benchmarked to international prices, inflation rebates, a lower out-of-pocket cap, and new dental, vision, and hearing coverage. The honest trade-off is that the price pressure falls entirely on brand-name manufacturers, and there is a plausible risk that lower expected returns on top-selling drugs could reduce some future drug development; opponents tried to condition implementation on exactly that question and were voted down. The design also has real weaknesses, including the extreme excise tax as the backstop and the bar on judicial review of price determinations. On balance, the consumer benefits were substantial and immediate, while the innovation cost was uncertain and contested.

outcome.mechanism: Received in the Senate on December 16, 2019, read twice and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 521) on September 8, 2020, but never brought to a Senate floor vote; the bill died when the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was referred to three House committees; all three reported it amended (Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means on December 6, 2019, and Education and Labor on December 9, 2019), and it was placed on the Union Calendar.

The House considered the bill under a structured rule (H. Res. 758) on December 11-12, 2019, adopted a set of amendments in the Committee of the Whole, and rejected a Republican motion to recommit 196-226 before passing it.
Final House passage was 230-192 on December 12, 2019: 228 Democrats and 2 Republicans voted yes; 191 Republicans, no Democrats, and 1 Independent voted no.

The Senate received the bill on December 16, 2019, read it the first time on August 13, 2020, and read it the second time on September 8, 2020, placing it on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 521. No further Senate action was taken before the Congress ended.

key_actors.name: Senate Majority Leader and Senate leadership
key_actors.role: Controlled the Senate floor calendar, 116th Congress (Republican-led Senate)
key_actors.what_they_did: Allowed H.R. 3 to sit on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 521) from September 8, 2020 until the Congress ended on January 3, 2021, without scheduling any debate or vote.

key_actors.name: Rep. Frank Pallone, Jr.
key_actors.what_they_did: Introduced the Elijah E. Cummings Lower Drug Costs Now Act on September 19, 2019 and shepherded it through House committee consideration and floor passage.

key_actors.name: House members voting on passage
key_actors.what_they_did: Passed the bill 230-192 on December 12, 2019, with near-unanimous Democratic support (228-0) and 2 Republican yes votes.

key_actors.name: Chairs of the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Labor Committees
key_actors.role: Committee chairs with jurisdiction over the bill
key_actors.what_they_did: Held markups in October 2019 and reported the bill amended in three parts (H. Rept. 116-324, Parts I-III) in December 2019, clearing it for floor action.

key_actors.name: Rep. Fred Upton
key_actors.role: U.S. Representative (R-MI), motion to recommit sponsor
key_actors.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions to delay its effective date until HHS certified the provisions were not projected to reduce new drug applications for unmet medical needs and life-saving cures; the motion failed 196-226.
